description: Multi-dimensional adversarial review of a diff or capability: correctness, security, and spec compliance, with every finding adversarially verified before it is reported.

findings.title: updateMission checks the topic-change rule before field validation, so an invalid request can get 409 instead of 400
findings.evidence: `if (topicId != null && topics.find(topicId) != null) { MissionRules.topicChange(stored, topicId)?.let { throw conflicts.of(it, stored) } }` runs before `validate(draft, stored)`. If a save changes the topic of a non-empty mission and also has a bad position or malformed task ids, the admin gets the 409 'remove its tasks first' and none of the field errors. TaskService.update does it the other way round (`validate(draft)` first, then `MissionRules.taskEdit`), so the two endpoints rank refusals differently.
findings.suggestion: Call `validate(draft, stored)` first, then `topicChange` on the validated `content.topicId`, then `edit`. Field errors (400) then always come before state conflicts (409), as they do for tasks.

findings.title: Mission reads are not transactional, so mission row and task list come from separate snapshots
findings.evidence: `fun list()` and `fun get(id)` have no `@Transactional`. `JdbcMissionStore.find/list` reads `mission` in one statement and `mission_task` in a second one (`withTasks`), and each runs in autocommit. If an update or task delete commits between them, the response can pair the old topic and position with the new task list. `view()` then makes two more separate `usage` calls.
findings.suggestion: Mark `list`/`get` `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` (as ServedContentService already is) so all of these reads use one transaction. Under READ COMMITTED that is still not a single snapshot; if exact consistency matters, use REPEATABLE READ or read the mission and its tasks in one query.

findings.title: Unpublishable conflict lists a task that is both draft and graphic twice in the detail
findings.evidence: `MissionRules.blockers` fills `drafts` and `graphic` independently, so a DRAFT GRAPHIC task is in both lists. The `mission-drafts-graphic` branch builds `listOf(tasks(b.drafts), tasks(b.graphic))`, so the detail names that task under 'Still drafts' and again under 'Graphic'. Only the `conflicts` ids are de-duplicated (`b.tasks()`).
findings.suggestion: Either accept this as intended (both statements are true) or exclude graphic tasks from the drafts list (or the reverse) when building the message, and add a test for a draft+graphic task.

findings.title: Conflict entity names are hard-coded English fragments outside the message catalog
findings.evidence: `return "$topic, mission ${mission.content.position}"` and `"task ${ref.taskNo}${ref.subPart.orEmpty()}, page ${ref.page}"` are built in code and passed as `{0}`/`{1}` into catalog messages. All other user-visible text is in `messages.properties`, so these words will not follow a future locale catalog. The `"?"` fallback for a missing topic also reaches the admin.
findings.suggestion: Move the name patterns to catalog keys (e.g. `content.name.mission={0}, mission {1}`, `content.name.task=task {0}, page {1}`) and format them with the request locale through ContentProblems.

findings.title: MissionRules.taskStatus takes a `task` parameter it never reads
findings.evidence: `fun taskStatus(task: Task, status: PublishStatus, missions: List<Mission>): Refusal?` only looks at `status` and `missions`. The signature suggests the current task state matters when it does not. Note that a DRAFT task already in a published mission, which the invariant should prevent, would also be refused.
findings.suggestion: Remove the unused parameter, or use it explicitly (e.g. skip the check when `task.status == status`) so the code says what it means.

findings.title: Mission list calls the usage port twice per mission (N+1 once practice implements ContentUsage)
findings.evidence: `list()` maps every mission through `view()`, which calls `usage.attemptCounts(ids)` and `usage.usedTasks(ids)` separately. With `ContentUsage.NONE` this costs nothing. With the slice-7 implementation, listing M missions runs 2·M usage queries. `TaskService.facts` likewise calls `usedTasks` and `attemptCounts` separately for one task.
findings.suggestion: In `list()`, collect every task id once, call `attemptCounts` and `usedTasks` once each, then build the views from the two results. Consider one port method that returns both facts.

findings.title: FR-12 child-facing scenarios are unverified, yet the plan closes FR-12 in slice 6 and its acceptance contract is artifact-ok
findings.evidence: Coverage: 40 scenarios: 35 implemented, 5 partial, 0 missing, 0 contradicted. The 5 partial scenarios are all here. Store spec 'Draft and published status' has two scenarios. 'Draft mission is not served': '...WHEN the child opens HQ THEN the mission is not listed and its tasks cannot be requested'. 'Published task outside any published mission': '...refused as not found'. 'Graphic tasks are never served in MVP' has two more: 'Published graphic task requested by id' → 'HTTP 404 ... application/problem+json', and 'Graphic task inside a draft mission' → 'both requests are answered with HTTP 404, and HQ lists neither M nor G'. 'Publish a valid mission' ends with '...and the child sees it on HQ'. In code, only the module query `ServedContentService` (src/main/kotlin/cz/doucko/content/application/ServedContentService.kt:175-190) exists, and no child endpoint consumes it. design.md:14-17 and :24-25 defer the 404 and HQ behaviour to slice 7. Yet contract/docs/mvp-capability-plan.md:259 assigns `| FR-12 | authoring-missions | backend |` to slice 6 only, and acceptance-contracts.json marks FR-12 `artifact-ok` on MissionApiTest.kt, which tests only the query (MissionApiTest.kt:684).
findings.suggestion: Amend the capability plan so FR-12 (and FR-5 serving) also travel with slice 7 (practice-flow), or add an explicit carry-over item to the slice-7 change. Keep the FR-12 acceptance status out of a final 'done' until the child 404/HQ scenarios have an executable test. Note the deferral in docs/current-state.md 'Scope NOT delivered' when task 5.5 is done.

findings.title: FR-56 usage guard is inert in the running app (ContentUsage.NONE), but FR-56 is planned and marked artifact-ok as fully delivered in slice 6
findings.evidence: The spec delta says: '`deleteTask` SHALL be 409 ... while any attempt, problem report or opened hint references it (FR-56, CA-D22) ... `AdminTask.attemptCount` ... `AdminMission.hasAttempts` ... SHALL report the same facts.' In code, `MissionService`/`TaskService` resolve `usageProvider.getIfAvailable { ContentUsage.NONE }` (MissionService.kt:39, TaskService.kt:90). No production bean exists, so in the app `usedTasks` is always empty, `attemptCount` is always 0, `hasAttempts` is always false, and the usage branch never fires. The guard logic is tested only with a fake (MissionApiTest.kt:575-659, MissionsIT.kt:190). design.md:26-29 documents this as a non-goal, but plan row `| FR-56 | authoring-missions | backend |` (mvp-capability-plan.md:293) has no slice-7 follow-up, and the acceptance contract is `artifact-ok`.
findings.suggestion: Record the real ContentUsage adapter as a slice-7 obligation tied to FR-56: add it to the plan row or to the slice-7 change tasks. Add an IT there that seeds a real attempt, report or opened hint and expects 409 on deleteTask/deleteMission.

findings.title: 409 `conflicts` for mission-topic-locked and last-task holds the mission's own id, which the contract defines as the blocking entities
findings.evidence: openapi.yaml:1144-1146 defines `conflicts`: 'Ids of the entities that block the action (e.g. the draft task blocking a mission publish)'. In code, `Refusal.LastTask -> ContentConflict("mission-last-task", ..., listOf(m.id))` and `Refusal.TopicLocked -> ContentConflict("mission-topic-locked", emptyList(), listOfNotNull(mission?.id))` (Conflicts.kt:48-55). The id returned is the mission being edited, not the tasks that block the topic change. This is documented only in design.md:105,109, not in the spec delta or the OpenAPI.
findings.suggestion: Either return the mission's task ids for TopicLocked (they are what blocks CA-D10), or amend the OpenAPI `conflicts` description and the spec delta to say that for a self-blocking rule it holds the edited mission id. The frontend relies on these shapes.

findings.title: Mission topic-lock message does not name the mission, unlike the other publishing-rule refusals
findings.evidence: The store spec 'Mission publishing rules' (spec.md:822-834) says: 'The edit rules that keep it, each refused with a message naming the mission to unpublish first, are these: ... A mission's topic SHALL change only while the mission has no tasks...' In code, `content.conflict.mission-topic-locked=The topic can only change while the mission is empty. Remove its tasks first.` takes no argument, and `Conflicts.of(TopicLocked)` passes `emptyList()` as args (Conflicts.kt:53-54). The scenario 'Changing the topic of a non-empty mission' only requires 'a message that the topic can only change while the mission is empty', so this is borderline.
findings.suggestion: Pass `name(mission)` and include it in the message (e.g. 'Desetinná čísla, mission 1'). Alternatively, amend the rule-list sentence in the store spec so the 'naming the mission' wording does not apply to the CA-D10 mission-topic rule.

findings.title: Topic-change refusal is checked before field validation, so a request with field errors can get 409 instead of 400
findings.evidence: The spec delta says: 'A refusal SHALL be 400 with `errors[].field` (`topicId`, `position`, `taskIds`, `taskIds[i]`)'. In code, `update` runs `MissionRules.topicChange(stored, topicId)?.let { throw conflicts.of(it, stored) }` before `validate(draft, stored)` (MissionService.kt:60-64). A PUT that changes the topic of a non-empty mission and also has, say, position `0` or 51 tasks gets 409 'mission-topic-locked' and no field errors. design.md decision 4 ('checked before the per-task topic rule') explains the intent, but no spec or OpenAPI text states the precedence over unrelated field errors.
findings.suggestion: Either validate the non-topic fields first, or document the precedence ('409 topic-lock takes precedence over field rules') in the spec delta or the updateMission OpenAPI description, and add a test that pins it.

findings.title: Grade-only change guard (CA-D10) has no test of its own
findings.evidence: The spec delta says: 'An `updateTask` that changes the topic or the grade SHALL be 409 while the task is in any mission'. In code, `MissionRules.taskEdit` checks `updated.topicId != current.topicId || updated.grade != current.grade` (Missions.kt:234). The only test changes both together: `taskEdit(c, c.copy(grade = 7, topicId = Topics.GRADE7), listOf(a))` (MissionRulesTest.kt:223). The `|| grade` branch alone is never tested, and the web test at MissionApiTest.kt:540 covers only the topic change.
findings.suggestion: Add a MissionRulesTest case with `c.copy(grade = 7)` and the same topic, expecting `TaskTopicInMissions`. This keeps the grade half of the CA-D10 guard tested.

result.reasoning:
The order the finding describes is real: `MissionService.update` (lines 60–64) calls `MissionRules.topicChange` before `validate(draft, stored)`. So a request that changes the topic of a non-empty mission and also has a bad position gets only the 409. But this order is deliberate and needed. It is not a correctness bug.

Why the order matters: `MissionRules.validate` → `tasks()` (Missions.kt:171) adds a 400 field error `task-topic` for every task id whose topic differs from the requested topic. The usual way to try a topic change is to re-save the mission with a new topicId and its current taskIds. Those tasks all belong to the old topic. With the suggested fix (validate first), that request would always fail validation with N `taskIds[i]: task-topic` 400 errors. It would never reach `topicChange`, so the CA-D10 refusal `mission-topic-locked` ('The topic can only change while the mission is empty. Remove its tasks first.') would be unreachable in the main scenario it exists for. The guard `topics.find(topicId) != null` exists so the early check runs only when the topic is valid and known. An unknown or malformed topic still goes to validation and gets a 400. That shows the order was designed on purpose.

The comparison with TaskService doesn't hold. When a task changes topic, the task's own field rules don't fail. When a mission changes topic, the kept taskIds fail FR-9 field validation, so the state conflict has to come first. The remaining effect is minor: in a request that is already refused, a bad position is reported after the 409 instead of with it. That only changes which error the admin sees first; nothing wrong is stored. The suggested fix would make things worse. Refuted.

The finding describes the code correctly but gets the consequence wrong. In MissionService.update (lines 58-65, not 666), topicChange runs before validate(draft, stored). So a topic change on a non-empty mission that also has a bad position returns 409 instead of 400. That part is reproducible.

The ordering is deliberate, though, and the suggested fix would break the CA-D10 refusal. MissionRules.validate (Missions.kt:171) adds a `task-topic` 400 error for every listed task whose topic differs from the requested topic. The normal case for CA-D10 is an admin changing the topic while sending back the mission's existing task ids. Those tasks all belong to the old topic, so with validate run first every such request would get a 400 list of `task-topic` errors for each task. The 409 TopicLocked ("remove its tasks first") would then almost never be reached. It would only fire if the admin also swapped in tasks from the new topic, and those would be rejected anyway because the stored tasks are still in the mission. The current order puts the one actionable message first and only when the target topic exists (`topics.find(topicId) != null`); field errors still come back once the topic issue is fixed.

TaskService ranks refusals differently because a task has no matching cascade of field errors. That difference is not an inconsistency defect. No user or attacker gets anything from this: it is an admin-only endpoint, nothing is stored on either path, and the admin only sees the problems one round at a time. At most this is a stylistic note, and the proposed change would make things worse.

I could not refute the finding. The mechanism is real; only the cited line number is wrong. MissionService.kt is about 130 lines long, so line 647 does not exist; the relevant code is lines 41–43 and 117–122.

- **No transaction on the reads.** `MissionService` has no class-level `@Transactional`. Only the write methods are annotated (lines 45, 53, 71, 86). `list()` and `get()` (lines 41/43) are not.
- **Two separate statements.** `JdbcMissionStore.list`/`find` (lines 22–31) run the `mission` SELECT through `JdbcClient`. `withTasks` (lines 121–131) then runs a second SELECT on `mission_task`. With no surrounding transaction, each statement runs in autocommit.
- **The writes can land in between.** `update()` rewrites the mission row and its whole task list in one transaction. `removeTask` deletes and renumbers `mission_task` rows. If either commits between the two reads, the response can combine the old topic/position with the new task list.
- **More reads in `view()`.** `view()` (lines 121–122) makes two more separate `usage` calls (`attemptCounts`, `usedTasks`). These can also disagree with the task list, so `hasAttempts` and `deletable` could be inconsistent.

Nothing else covers this. There is no class-level transaction, no read lock, and no single-query join. `ServedContentService` does have `@Transactional(readOnly = true)`, which shows the codebase uses that pattern where it wants it.

The impact is small. These are admin-only authoring reads, the window is a few milliseconds, and the wrong result lasts only for that one response; nothing wrong is stored. The finding itself correctly says the suggested fix is partial: under Postgres's default READ COMMITTED isolation, each statement still gets its own snapshot. Minor severity is appropriate.

The code does what the finding says, but it's hard to reproduce and does no lasting harm. The cited line is wrong: MissionService.kt is about 130 lines long, and the code is at lines 41–43 (`list()` / `get()`), not 647.

Confirmed in code:
- `list()` and `get()` have no `@Transactional`, and there is no class-level annotation on `MissionService` (lines 30–43).
- `JdbcMissionStore.list/find` reads `mission` in one statement, then `withTasks` (JdbcMissionStore.kt:121–131) runs a separate `SELECT … FROM mission_task`. Each statement auto-commits on its own.
- `view()` (lines 117–122) then makes two more separate `usage` calls (`attemptCounts`, `usedTasks`).
- A write that commits between those statements could therefore produce a mixed response. The writes (`update` / `delete`) do commit atomically, in a transaction after `lock.exclusive()`.

Why it is hardly reachable in practice:
- These are admin-only endpoints (MissionController), and the app has a single admin (the parent).
- To see the problem, that admin would need two clients, such as two browser tabs: one saving a mission at the exact moment the other's list/get falls into the microsecond gap between two SELECTs.
- The outcome is only a stale or mixed read model in one HTTP response. Nothing is stored and no decision depends on it. Every write path takes the exclusive content lock and reads again inside its own transaction (lines 45–90), so a mixed GET cannot cause a bad write. The next read is correct.
- There is no security angle: no answer key leaks, and no child endpoint is involved.

The suggested fix is also weak, as the finding itself admits. `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` under Postgres's default READ COMMITTED still takes a fresh snapshot for each statement, so it would not close the gap. Only REPEATABLE READ or a single query would.

The mechanism is real, so this is not refuted. But the trigger is a near-impossible race, the effect is a one-off stale display that fixes itself, and the fix as proposed doesn't fix it. It belongs at nit/informational level, not minor.

The unused parameter is real, but the finding does not show a correctness defect. The cited line is also wrong: the function is at Missions.kt:218 (the file is about 250 lines), not line 1200.

What the code does: `taskStatus(task, status, missions)` returns null unless `status == DRAFT`. When it is DRAFT, it returns `TaskDraftInPublished` if any of the given missions are published. `task` is never read. The only production caller is `TaskService.setStatus` (TaskService.kt:162). It takes the exclusive lock, loads `current`, runs the rule, and writes only if `current.status != status`.

Why this is not a correctness bug:
1. **The FR-57 rule works without `task`.** The rule is: a task in a published mission cannot become DRAFT. That depends only on the target status and the missions containing the task. Nothing about the current task changes the answer.
2. **The suggested short-circuit would weaken the guard.** Skipping the check when `task.status == status` matters only for a DRAFT→DRAFT request on a task that is already in a published mission. The finding admits the invariant prevents that state: publishing a mission or adding a task to one requires published tasks (`blockers`/`CannotJoin`). If the state appeared anyway through corruption or a race, refusing the no-op is the safer, consistent behaviour, and accepting it would hide the broken invariant.
3. **Tests pin the behaviour.** `MissionRulesTest:205-208` and `MissionApiTest:415/422` check the refuse and allow cases, and they match the spec.

So the claimed mechanism, "the signature suggests the current state matters when it does not", is a readability point (an unused parameter that may trigger a compiler warning), not wrong behaviour. Under the correctness lens there is nothing to fix. At most it is a style or cleanup nit, so if it is kept at all it should go under maintainability, not correctness.

The finding is correct, though the line number is wrong. The function is at Missions.kt:218, not line 1200. `fun taskStatus(task: Task, status: PublishStatus, missions: List<Mission>)` never reads `task`. Its body only checks `status != DRAFT` and `missions.published()`. The only production caller passes `current` (TaskService.kt:162). The unit tests in MissionRulesTest.kt:205-208 pass `t`, but the result never depends on it.

There is no user-visible failure. The finding's side note does describe real behaviour: a DRAFT→DRAFT request for a task in a published mission would be refused, because `task.status` is never checked. But that can only happen if a published mission contains a draft task, which the publishing invariant is meant to prevent. And refusing the request would be harmless anyway.

So this is a real but cosmetic issue: a misleading signature with no reachable bug. It stays at minor severity.
